Choose where Nostr can actually find you.

Your key owns the identity, but relays decide where signed events can be written, read, searched, filtered and recovered. A good relay setup gives you reach without pretending one endpoint is the whole network.
Where does your client publish events?
Where do clients look for people and replies?
What does the relay accept, reject or require?
Can you move when an operator changes the rules?
A relay is a place with rules, not a random URL.

Use this hub when a feed looks empty, a client asks for relay settings, a paid relay appears, a local community needs memory, or a product quietly depends on infrastructure you have not inspected yet. You will not get a useful answer from a giant endpoint list alone; you need to know what job each relay does, what policy it declares, what it stores, what it refuses and how easily you can leave.

children: Start with the real machinery: your client sends signed events, relays decide what they accept, and other clients ask those relays what they can read. Once you see that loop, blank feeds and missing replies stop feeling mysterious.

Do not copy a fashionable relay list as if every endpoint does the same work. Choose a small set for reach, archive, search, local rooms, wallet traffic, paid reliability and experiments you can remove again.

NIP-11 is the relay's public face: name, software, supported NIPs, limits, contacts and payment hints. It will not prove honesty, but it tells you whether the operator even bothers to explain the room you are entering.

NIP-42 matters when a relay asks your key to prove access without handing over your private key. You should know who asks, why the challenge appears, what you are signing and whether the client makes that moment legible.

NIP-65 gives other clients a better hint about where you write and where you read. A clean list makes you easier to find; a bloated list turns discovery into guesswork and makes every client pay for your old experiments.

Outbox discovery asks where a person actually publishes instead of assuming one global relay can answer for everyone. That one shift changes feed design, social discovery, migration and how clients recover context.

Free, paid, invite-only and community relays all make different promises. When money appears, inspect what you are buying: lower spam, storage, search, support, admission, reputation, or simply the operator's time.
Open the software, monitors, NIPs and directories before repeating a relay claim. The source trail is where marketing language either becomes testable infrastructure or quietly falls apart.
